topics.title: Classroom translations
topics.text:
A class that consists of 24 students, arranged in a 6 by 4 array, is playing a game. A ball is given to the student sitting at the top left corner of the array. Define a passing to be a movement of the ball $x$ units up and $y$ units to the right; $x,y\in \mathbb{Z}$. This student picks a passing that will be carried on throughout the game; i.e. the next person who receives the ball will pass it on in the same fashion



Here are two different possibilities when the ball reaches an edge of the classroom.



First possibility is that it reflects: For example, if the passing was $x=1, y=1$ and the ball was passed from $1,3$ to $0,4$, it would then reflect to position $1,5$



Second possibility is that it goes through: For example, if the passing was $x=1,y=1$ and the ball was passed from $1,3$ to $0,4$, it would then go through the array, to the other side where it reaches student at $4, 5$.



In each of these scenarios, what is the maximum number of students that can hold the ball?

topics.title: What makes a Carmichael Number?
topics.text:
This question regards Carmichael Numbers.



There is a test for primes where you put in any value of $x$  and put it into $x^p-x$ where that expression is divisible by $x$ is divisble by $x$. We won't regard Fermat Liars and Witnesses.



Carmichael Numbers pass the test for every value of $x$ (when $x$ is a Carmichael Number) until $x$ (So, since $561$ is a Carmichael Number, $x^{560}-x$ will always be divisible by $561$ where $561>x.$)

topics.title: k Does 0.99999... = 1?
topics.text:
So, let's say that we have to convert $0.\overline 999999$. Pretty confusing right? But, we have found out how we can successfully say that we have proof that $0.\overline 9999 = 1$. Here's how:

So, lets say that $x=0.\overline999$, okay. Then we should multiply this by about $1000$, or more zeroes added if you please. Next, you should move the decimal, and you get $1000x = 999.\overline999$. Next, we subtract the original $x$ from it, and we get $1000x-x=999.\overline999-0.\overline999$, and this is gives use $999$. Next, to get $x$ as a fraction, we do $\frac{999}{999}$. We have $999$ as our denominator because we have $999x$, remember? Finally, we actually divide and we get $999/999 = 1$! Amazing! And, this is how to prove that $0.\overline999$ is $1$

Post on this thread if you have something to say. Otherwise, I will be posting some theories that some people who have devoted their full life to solve this. Please feel free to post here!

topics.title: Puzzling Question (Combinatorics)
topics.text:
This problem has driven me insane today...



(PLEASE read to the end! I know you got 64 already....)



Let's say we have a grid of $P$s and $O$s, arranged like this:$$P$$$$P \text{         } O  \text{         } P$$$$P  \text{         } O  \text{         } P  \text{         } O  \text{         } P$$$$P  \text{         } O  \text{          } P$$$$P$$

How many times are the word $POP$ in the grid, if one $POP$ can use the same $P$ as it's starting and ending $P$, and $POP$ doesn't have to be in a straight line?



This would be okay:$$...  \text{           } P$$$$P  \text{              } O$$

---



Take a minute to think.  3...2...1...



---



So this is the "official" solution: $64$.  It's probably what you came up with.  How did we get $64$?



Let's start with the center $O$.  There are 4 $O$s in the grid.  As you have probably noticed, each $O$ has 4 $P$s surrounding it, positioned like this: $$...  \text{    } P  \text{    } ...$$$$ P  \text{    } O  \text{    } P$$$$... \text{    } P  \text{    } ...$$

Since you can use the same $P$ twice, you have $4$ choices for the first $P$, and $4$ again for the second $P$.  This

means that each $O$ has $16$ $POP$s with it as the center $O$, and since there are four $O$s with the same number and configuration of $P$s around them, the answer is $64$.



---



Pretty obvious, right?  Well, some deeper thinking lead to this:



---



Let's skip doing the fancy math.  Instead, let's make sure we're right by doing this out by "hand" (or keyboard....)



Here, we revisit this diagram, now with numbered $P$s: $$...  \text{    } P_1  \text{    } ...$$$$ \text{    } P_2  \text{    } O  \text{    } P_3$$$$ ...  \text{    } P_4  \text{    } ...$$

Since we can use the same $P$ twice, each $P$ in the diagram below has two "variants", let's say: $P$ and $P^{'}$.  We only use these separately while using the same $P$ for both $P$s in the word $POP$.



Here is a list of all the possible $POP$s:



It's big: long story short, we get 20 POPs! How odd!$$1: P_1 O P^{`}_1$$$$2: P^{`}_1 O P_1$$$$3: P_2 O P^{`}_2$$$$4: P^{`}_2 O P_2$$$$5: P_3 O P^{`}_3$$$$6: P^{`}_3 O P_3$$$$7: P_4 O P^{`}_4$$$$8: P^{`}_4 O P_4$$$$9: P_1 O P_2$$$$10: P_1 O P_3$$$$11: P_1 O P_4$$$$12: P_2 O P_1$$$$13: P_2 O P_3$$$$14: P_2 O P_4$$$$15: P_3 O P_1$$$$16: P_3 O P_2$$$$17: P_3 O P_4$$$$18: P_4 O P_1$$$$19: P_4 O P_2$$$$20: P_4 O P_3$$




Now, while you might think that counting $P^{'}_1 O P_1$ different from $P_1 O P^{'}_1$ is simply absurd, however "technically" true it is, a more important question is raised: why are these two results different?



As you may have noticed, every $POP$ that uses different $P$s is counted twice, once forwards once backwards, but each $POP$ that uses the same $P$ is counted once.  That simply doesn't work!



If we said that backwards vs. forwards $POP$ that uses the same letters are different, then why shouldn't that be applied to single-P $POP$s?  If so, we get 80.



But, of course, counting that $POP$ twice seems really odd, so if you counted same letter $POP$s as only one, no matter if its forwards or backwards, then you get 40.



What a poorly worded question.

When the girl reaches the end, the boy has covered only two-fifths of the length of the walkway. What is the ratio of the walkway's rate to a girl and a boy's walking speed?

topics.title: MathCounts problem
topics.text: Janelle averages 40 kilometers per hour biking on level ground. She averages 60% of her level ground speed riding uphill, and she averages 120% of her level-ground speed riding downhill. The course is level for 5 kilometers, uphill for 6 kilometers, and then downhill for 6 kilometers. How many kilometers per hour is her average speed for the entire course?

topics.title: Probability of equal heads and tails
topics.text:
Suppose that mathguy5041 flips 1232 fair coins. What is the reciprocal of the probability that he gets an equal number of heads and tails? Round your answer to the nearest integer.



I wrote this problem, try to do it without a calculator. (Yes, it's possible. Try to get an approximation, no need for an exact answer.)



hintThe unrounded answer is EXTREMELY CLOSE to an integer. (Can you figure out why?) Think about the prime factorization of 1232.

topics.title: Paradoxes
topics.text:
We can express $1$ as $2-1$. And express that $1$ as $2-1$. Now we have $2-(2-1)=1$. So, $(2-(2-(2-1)=2$. And...

$(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-1)))$. Keep on doing this infinetly and...

$(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2-(2...-2-2-1=1$. But... the $2$s repeat infinetly so you never get to $1$! So, we can keep removing the parentheses because they now don't matter and get $2-2-2-2-2-2-2-2-2-2-2-2-2-2...=1$.



So, $-\infty=1$.



How do I do this?



P.S. Also, the twos will always make $0$ and always cancel everything so either $-\infty=1$ or $2=1$.
